questions.prompt: Walk through how ww27 decides which API contract a request is served under: where the version can come from, how live rollout settings are applied, who is let through, and what the code does with a version string it does not recognise.

keyPoints.text: Resolution order is an explicit (path) version, then the x-api-version header, then the ?version query parameter, and only then the registry's default.

An unregistered string makes getRequestedVersion throw badRequest instead of quietly serving the default; but the profile routes' error path re-resolves the version from the same request, so the senior review records that the caller actually sees a framework 500, not the intended 400.
buildApiContext resolves the session, then the requested version, then the EFFECTIVE definition, and only then checks access, so a runtime rollout change actually takes effect.
The effective definition is the static registry entry with its rollout replaced by the catalog's runtime record when one exists.

Access: ADMIN, SUPPORT and ANALYST always pass; otherwise an allowlisted client passes; otherwise the client's deterministic bucket must fall below the rollout percentage, or the request is refused with 403.
The rollout route narrows its raw path segment with toApiVersionId before building context, because a typed parameter is still just a string at runtime.
keyPoints.quote: Runtime version checks protect the same boundary for path parameters, which are strings even when the function signature narrows them.

keyPoints.text: Types and runtime checks do different jobs: the union narrows code paths, the check stops a bad string before anything is written.
keyPoints.quote: A discriminated version contract lets TypeScript narrow v1 and v2 safely; a runtime version check rejects unknown strings before an operational write.

questions.prompt: Explain how ww27's adapters serve two public contracts from one canonical customer profile: what each direction of translation does, where the legacy contract cannot carry the canonical state, and how errors are kept version-neutral. Name one place where the adapter and the schema disagree.

keyPoints.text: Version vocabulary stops at the adapter; services and repositories only ever see canonical fields.
keyPoints.quote: The canonical model is the stable seam: version-specific names and statuses should not leak into repository or service policy.

keyPoints.text: A v1 create cannot express consent at all, so the adapter stores marketingOptIn as false, and the legacy inactive status is stored as SUSPENDED.
On the way out, the four canonical lifecycle states are collapsed into two legacy words, so a v1 reader cannot tell SUSPENDED from ARCHIVED.
Each version has its own strict zod schema, selected by the resolved version, so a field from the other contract is rejected instead of silently ignored.
Failures are the one shape both versions share.
keyPoints.quote: A malformed v1 request should receive the same safe error envelope as a malformed v2 request, while the success body differs by version.

keyPoints.text: toErrorResponse renders a ZodError as 400 VALIDATION_ERROR and anything unrecognised as 500, both through jsonWithVersionHeaders.

Disagreement: isV2Update only recognises a v2 patch by name, lifecycleState or marketingOptIn, so a schema-valid v2 patch carrying only email or externalReference is refused by the adapter with a plain Error, which the error mapper turns into a 500.

questions.prompt: Defend or indict this claim: "ww27 tells v1 clients they are on a deprecated contract, and operators can tell when it is safe to retire it." Cover the response signals, the telemetry, the rollout controls and the client side.

keyPoints.text: Every response carries x-api-version and x-api-lifecycle; a DEPRECATED version also gets Deprecation: true and a 299 Warning naming the sunset date.
Error responses get the same headers, because toErrorResponse builds them with jsonWithVersionHeaders too.
The Sunset header is the registry's bare date rather than an HTTP-date, and the stored deprecation date is never sent, so a strict client may miss both.
recordVersionUsage writes a usage row for successes and failures alike, with deprecationFired set for a deprecated version; those rows are the evidence for who still calls v1.

A rollout change is ADMIN-only, validated (integer percentage 0-100, non-empty unique allowlist ids, known version) before the write, and audited; if the audit write fails the previous rollout is restored, though a crash between the two writes still leaves an unaudited change.
Rollout input is checked before anything is persisted, not discovered later at override time.
keyPoints.quote: Rollout validation similarly belongs before repository writes

keyPoints.text: Client side, fetchJson parses every success body as JSON; the codebase map's rule that a 204 must not be parsed means a future no-content endpoint would break this helper.
